Any plans on upstreaming any of this to mathlib?

@Kevin Buzzard , as someone who is also doing these kind of autoformalization experiments, I am very curious to see that you would like this kind of AI-slop formalization upstreamed. Considering that even a O(100 LOC) mathlib PR often takes several rounds of revisions, I do not see how it would be possible to upstream even a 10k LOC project in mathlib at the moment. One data point: two months ago I autoformalized the converge of the Forward Euler Method, about 200 LOC. I significantly cleaned up the code semi-manually and split into two PRs but still stuck in the review process. I have two other autoformalization projects with O(1k-10k LOC), one about the equilibrium of a PDE, another on sheaf cohomology, but I do not see a way to upstream any of it to mathlib at the moment.

We seriously need sloplib!

Well I looked at the code and it didn't look too bad, although some proofs were far too long (200+ lines). I agree that upstreaming would be an extremely slow process. I agree that the community is going to have to figure out a place to put this stuff. For me one key question is: will this code still compile with current mathlib this time next year, or will it just have rotted? Who cares about this code enough to keep it alive?

There are now dozens of these kind of large scale autoformalization projects. If we had sloplib, we would put them all there, maybe with an AI agent working through the version bumping when Lean version changes. But right now there is nothing to do with these project but have them rot.

I would love for a prominent member of the community (you?) to just make a fork of mathlib, change review guidelines to something extremely basic (does it compile at default heartbeats and are all proofs below 200 lines? If yes, PR gets merges automatically) in order to give a place for all these AI-slop autoformalization projects.
Vasily Ilin it sounds like you're looking for merely-true
@Snir Broshi , it's just an empty Lean repo at v4.24

But it's exactly the place you said you want to exist, everything that passed CI is auto-merged, and the point is to let AI bots loose on it.

If we had sloplib, we would put them all there, maybe with an AI agent working through the version bumping when Lean version changes.

I don't see the benefit of putting all of these projects in a monorepo if they don't conform to some shared style guide and principles, and LLMs are notoriously bad at sticking to principles (humans a bit better due to social credit, linters are best).

What I am surprised is that the conversation keeps being binary - human-only (or mostly?) mathlib vs sloplib. Surely, the truth is somewhere in the middle, where responsible AI usage powers mathlib - if the linux kernel is starting to get excited about AI usage why can't mathlib - https://www.theregister.com/2026/03/26/greg_kroahhartman_ai_kernel/ . Isn't the linux kernel similarly high-stakes high-quality codebase like mathlib? Note, that AI is powering both sides of the equation there - not only authoring but reviewing too.

2) "proof-of-quality"

can't this happen from your existing github repos

@Rado Kirov , it cannot, because

  1. the code in merely-true is actually true, i.e. it actually compiles. Most large-scale projects will stop compiling after one version bump.
  2. the code in merely-true is non-conflicting. It is likely that while projects A, B, and C compile separately but do not compile when put together even if they use the same Lean version (e.g. naming clashing).
  3. how would one even discover these random formalization projects? There is Lean Reservoir but it does not work well, e.g. algebraic-combinatorics that started this thread is not indexed, and my Clawrisotle also is not.
Good point, should add 3) compiles with newest version of lean and mathlib as a value prop for sloplib.

There is something to be said here, in terms of the intended audience.

On the one hand, the Lean "experts" that use AI , have some agent .md set up a certain way, and would likely sign post and get better results to refine (than they would otherwise get from such a repo).

On the other hand, longer tasks take a lot of time, and perhaps there is a benefit of saving compute by displaying such a repo.

It is really hard to say for sure, another issue for longer runs is : even if a deeper theorem is proven, a lot of AI code has been built up to that point that has been used to prove the deeper result.

And potentially such a large amount would have to be re-done that an expert may have saved more time with a more lightweight AI approach.

That being said for other more individual open source verification, where code quality and maintenance for new dependency versions /updating is less of an issue , what is merely true can be more plainly useful.
I have enabled CI on PRs from forks for https://github.com/merely-true/merely-true. It requires manual approval for first time contributors; please DM me if you need this.

I think merely-true is also interesting from the perspective of usage. Definitions / Theorems, which get used most from merely-true are the best candidates for upstreaming to mathlib, both from the perspective of usefulness (e.g. People use these formalizations in their projects) and "proof of quality". What does not get used, bit rots.

@Kim Morrison , https://github.com/merely-true/merely-true/pull/15 passes CI but is not merged. Same with my other PR.

Also, I have a couple of proposals:

  1. While we don't have much code in merely-true yet, I think it's worth it to bump to the latest Lean version. When bumping versions, I propose letting Claude adapt the code to the new version. In my experience it can solve most versioning issues. This way we'll have some continuity instead of starting from scratch at each version.
  2. Whatever aspects of code quality can be checked automatically should be enforced. For example, no file with >1k LOC, no proof with >100 LOC, standard mathlib linter (no LOC with >80 chars, docstrings for theorems, etc). As long as it does not take human reviewers' time, I don't see why not enforce better code quality.
  3. Most important: default heartbeats must be enforced. Otherwise merely-true will quickly exceed the 6h timeout of GH Actions CI and just stop compiling.
  4. Documentation: each PR must come with a README.md in the folder it adds. This directly contradicts the current rule of merely-true that non-lean files are not allowed. The reason I propose documentation is because it makes it easier to actually use merely-true in the future, e.g. for gradual upstreaming to mathlib or for other autoformalization projects to depend on it. Essentially, merely-true can be the sloplib that Kevin Buzzard proposed. For this to happen, we need documentation.

While we don't have much code in merely-true yet

On the other hand we are deluged with autoformalizations and I think there's plenty of evidence that the rate of the deluge is going to go up and up. Let's actively start telling people to target merely-true!

Hi all,

I'm one of the authors of the automatic textbook formalization work that @Fabian Glöckle shared here recently. I wanted to follow up — not with another announcement, but with a question for this community.

The discussion that followed Fabian's post was genuinely useful to us. Several of you raised points that we've been thinking about a lot:

  • @Kevin Buzzard's "what is the point" question — 130K lines that rot in a year aren't worth much
  • @Joseph Myers's point that large code dumps developed in private go badly, and that AI should help identify API gaps and upstream small lemmas incrementally
  • The broader concern about "slop": code that compiles but that no human understands or maintains

If I understand correctly, the hard part isn't closing proof goals and posting 130k LoC online; it's making the right design decisions, and building with the community.

So here's what we're thinking about for the next step: what if a swarm of agents could work on formalization targets in parallel, with humans supervising and steering?

The textbook project used ~30K agent calls. The next version of this won't be a single bot running as a pair programmer — it'll be many agents working tirelessly on different worktrees, with a human acting as supervisor.
The leverage is that one human supervisor can keep dozens of agents productive, instead of writing every proof themselves.

Here's what this could look like in practice:

  • A fleet of agents working on a formalization target in a public repo, each tackling a different lemma or section
  • When agents collectively get stuck on something — a design decision, a hard proof, a Mathlib API question — the problem gets escalated to a Zulip topic for human input
  • A human reviews, gives a high-level fix or design ruling, and the agents absorb that and keep going
  • The human doesn't need to write the Lean — they need to know what the right Lean would look like
  • The output is meant to be high-quality enough for merely-true, not a big dump with some arrogant X post.

We don't have the full system built yet — we're exploring what this could look like. Before going further, I'd genuinely like to know:

  1. Would this community be open to a supervised AI system occasionally escalating questions to a Zulip topic? (Clearly labeled as AI-generated, confined to its own topic, rate-limited — not flooding your streams. These would be curated questions, not raw agent output.)
  2. What formalization targets would actually be useful? We're thinking about targets where the output has lasting value — textbook companions that serve as educational resources, filling gaps in Mathlib's coverage, or building toward merely-true. Open to suggestions.
  3. What would make you actually want to answer the AI's questions? The pitch is that a 10-minute answer from you unblocks hours of agent-compute. We want to design the interaction so it's interesting and useful for the humans too.

Happy to discuss any of this. And if the answer is "please don't put a bot on our Zulip," that's useful feedback too.

I have a question regarding merely true: the idea is to have no human supervision at all? Building something faster than Mathlib seems relevant, but without any guardrails seems a bit dangerous if we want to ensure we do not have a lib that change the kernel behavior with some Evil.lean or mislead between two closely related concepts (e.g. between two different integrals, or spaces, before proving seemingly impressive results on the wrong object)

I understand that the current idea is to have only verified contributors, how do we get us/our bots validated?
Also the readme actually says that there would be a Zulip channel for AI? Is it live already?

[...] if we want to ensure we do not have a lib that change the kernel behavior with some Evil.lean or mislead between two closely related concepts

A repository like this that is robust against adversarial contributors will likely remain impossible for the foreseeable future.

Maybe some files could be somehow marked as "theorem statement files", which only contain theorems based on Mathlib definitions and no definitions of their own (assuming one could enforce something like that in a semi-automated way)? One could use comparator to check those.

One could provide some loogle-clone (sloogle?) for those theorems, so people who proved something useful for their work have a way to make that public in a reusable way (it's at a central place and keeps getting auto-maintained and updated) without having to go through Mathlib review (or maybe for showing what they have as a starting point for discussing the process for refactoring towards a potential Mathlib contribution). That seems a lot better than dumping a single .lean file on GitHub without even a toolchain-file, which seems to be happening quite a bit right now.

I'm thinking about licensing/authorship/copyright (not a lawyer, not legal advice, etc.)...

Suppose you're using AI to formalize a math paper of yours. Assuming that

  1. the resulting Lean code is a derivative work of the paper (which I'm not sure is legally true)
  2. you can claim no authorship for AI output

I think that you can still license the output under any license you choose, as long as you have copyright for the paper (which may change if the paper is published?!).

However, if in the course of the AI formalization the AI goes and downloads some papers from ArXiv and formalizes those, some files in your repository could be considered derivative works of those papers. Papers have different licenses, most requiring attribution but some prohibiting derivative works, and I'm not sure AIs always look this up and follow it. I think that even assuming that the AI informs you of the papers it used and compiles with the licenses there, the result is most likely incompatible with Apache 2.0 license.

So even leaving aside the question of "should we burn at the stake anyone who even considers taking someone else's paper and just formalizing it?" (which people will do and which I think would be at least legal when complying with the paper's license, e.g. including proper attribution), I think this part of the README:

Contributors agree to license their contributions under the Apache 2.0 License.

strictly speaking means that you have to instruct your AI not to search for other papers if you want to be able to PR to merely-true.

The broader question, even apart from what's legal, is what kinds of AI interactions with works of others we consider acceptable.

Now that we are actually talking about a sloplib-like library seriously, I would like to reiterate my proposal to make an honest effort to make it good:

  • I propose the name ai-mathlib because it's a mathematical library, made by AI. merely-true sounds like anything that's true belongs in it, which I do not believe to be the case.
  • I propose to ensure as high quality of code and documentation as possible without human review. Concretely, this means using the mathlib linter, additional linters for documentation, and LLM-based review like botbaki.
  • Each submission must be a finished self-contained project that can be described as "This project formalized X", where X is a significant piece of serious mathematics (a textbook, a theorem from a math paper, a well-known result, etc). This can be enforced by the LLM reviewer.

Additional context: https://github.com/merely-true/merely-true/pull/33.

I don't see a great way to avoid this other than letting it happen

A combination of LLM-based reviewer like botbaki and linters enforcing documentation?

@Bolton Bailey I just read your "Thoughts on AI Formal Codebase Maintenance". I was impressed by your idea to "set up a system where users/contributors submit their own metrics". Something like an autonomous democratic mathlib. My main concern is that:
(1) Certain metrics could easily be gamed by the system. For example, if a cost function includes "Total Lines of Code" then a bot could easily just bring an entire proof into a single-unreadable line.
(2) Mathematics is a highly specialized discipline. What makes a well-written geometry proof is not the same as what makes a well-written analysis proof. Allowing everyone to set up metrics for the entire codebase might have adverse effects. Better would be to let individual mathematicians to set up preferences for their own subfield.

In your write up, you mention that (1) can be solved by "tweaking" the metric over time. My main worry is that an ever-changing target brings with it an ever-changing codebase. There's no guarantee of backwards compatibility for projects that might depend on the library. There's also the problem of the potentially-infinite amount of energy/compute resources it would take to continually refactor code as optimal preferences change. Unless there is financial incentive to run AI reviewers/maintainers, I do not see how the work would actually get done, and I fear we would all drown in tech debt.

I definitely conceive the concept of a "metric" broadly enough that it could encompass different subfolders/parts of the library having different metrics consistent with the needs of particular mathematical subfields!

I agree that this tweaking process might lead to a lot of churn. This requires lots of resources, but at least in this case they will be compute resources rather than human time. Hi everyone, I am another coauthor of https://arxiv.org/html/2604.03071v1 and a colleague of @Vivien Cabannes at Meta.

As mentioned by Vivien, we are interested in contributing to the autoformalization community, and already have some projects underway. We have a question regarding licenses: what are the "good" licenses under which to release AI-generated formalizations? My understanding was that Apache 2 was ideal, but are other licenses, such as CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, acceptable?

I think the reason mathlib was Apache2 was simply "Lean is Apache2 so it's just easiest that way". And then the reason FLT was Apache2 was "Lean and mathlib are Apache2 and they seem to know what they're doing".
But I assume it might nonetheless be tricky to integrate codebases that operate under different licenses

I greatly enjoy working in an environment where I can just move code around between different parts of the ecosystem.

So I strongly suggest that you also use Apache 2.

If you don't want to (or can't), then please tell us why :wink:

Keep in mind that CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 is a very very restrictive license, particularly the "ND" part which basically forbids anyone from improving and possibly building on your work. So if your intent is to "contribute" to anything, this seems like a suboptimal choice. The Creative Commons people also recommend against using CC licenses for code, see the question "Can I apply a Creative Commons license to software?" at https://creativecommons.org/faq/

Keep in mind also that if your output is LLM-generated that what parts of it are copyrightable (ensuring parts of it did not regurgitate prior licensed work, along with the core question of whether what was outputted is at all copyrightable) are themselves fun questions (and then asking that about different countries' IP law...)

@Johan Commelin ideally, we would like to use the license that is most convenient for the community, but there are two constraints that we must consider:
